newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU clears Thyssen/Krupp flat steel venture.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU clears Thyssen/Krupp flat steel venture.

text.p: The European Commission said on Tuesday it had cleared a joint venture between German steel giants Thyssen Stahl AG and Krupp Hoesch Stahl AG in the flat steel sector.

The decision did not cover some other activities transferred to the joint venture, namely production of steel tubes and trading in fertilisers, which are covered by separate EU legislation, a Commission source told Reuters.

The two companies agreed earlier this year to pool their flat steel and other activities after Krupp's announcement of a hostile takeover of its archrival met with the resistance of Thyssen workers and German political leaders.

Despite the sheer size of the new company, the Commission said it would not be in a position to manipulate prices of flat steel given the strong competition from other European producers and the relative under-utilisation of production capacity.

It used provisions in the treaty of the European Coal and Steel Community to clear the deal. Trade in fertilisers, production of steel tubes and transport services are covered by the European law on merger control. The deadline for the EU to rule on this is August 11, the Commission source said.

The venture called Thyssen Krupp Stahl, which will be owned 60 percent by Thyssen and 40 percent by Krupp, will become the leading supplier of hot-rolled and cold-rolled flat steel in the European Union, the Commission said in a statement.

It will hold 16 percent of the European market for hot-rolled flat products, 13 percent of the market for uncoated flat products and between 12 and 30 percent for coated flat products. The products are used mainly in the car and building industries.
"On the relevant markets the parties to the concentration face competition from a number of other steel producers in the (European) Community," the Commission said in a statement.
It particularly singled out France's Usinor Sacilor, Italy's Riva/Ilva, British Steel, Cockerill Sambre of Belgium and Luxembourg's Arbed.

The Commission said the new company would also have a strong position in the distribution of steel products particularly in Germany where its market share varied between five and 18 percent. In the rest of the Union its share would not exceeed 10 percent, it said.

Krupp announced in March a hostile bid for Thyssen offering to pay 435 marks a share, or a premium of some 25 percent on the market price. Fears of huge job losses led the companies to engage in talks about forming a joint venture only days after the surprise announcement.
Thyssen shares were trading at 419 marks on Tuesday, one mark less on Monday's closing.
The joint venture deal was filed for EU regulatory approval on July 7.
